h1: Switching to brewing in your thirties or forties from another career
title: Switching to Brewing in Your 30s or 40s | Craft Beer School
desc: How to move into brewing in your thirties or forties: the honest trade-offs, the skills you already have and a sensible plan for making the switch.
teaser: Plenty of brewers started late. The ones who made it planned the move instead of jumping.
standfirst: Changing career in your thirties or forties is different from starting at twenty two. You have more to lose and more to offer. This guide covers the trade-offs and a practical way to make the switch into brewing.
sections:
Brewing has always attracted people from other careers. Engineers, chemists, chefs, bankers, IT professionals and teachers have all become good brewers. Many started in their thirties or forties, often after years of homebrewing.

Age itself is rarely the problem. The challenges are practical: money, family commitments, the physical work and starting again near the bottom of a new ladder. Face those honestly and the switch is very possible. Our guide to the move from homebrewer to pro brewer covers the path in more detail.

• Pay: entry level brewing jobs often pay less than an established mid-career salary. Plan for a drop, at least at first.
  • Hours: early starts, long brew days and weekend work are normal.
  • Physical work: lifting malt sacks, cleaning tanks and working in heat. It is manageable for most healthy adults, but it is real.
  • Status: you may report to a head brewer much younger than you. That works fine if you are open to learning from them.

If those trade-offs feel acceptable, keep reading. If they do not, consider a role that uses your current career inside a drinks company, for example in quality, data, finance or sales.
What you bring that a twenty year old does not

Experience counts for more than people expect. You already know how to work with colleagues, manage your time, handle pressure and solve problems. Depending on your background, you may bring skills a brewery badly needs:

  • Engineers understand pumps, chillers and control systems.
  • Scientists understand lab work and microbiology.
  • Finance people understand cost per litre and cash flow.
  • Managers understand rosters, training and people.
  • Chefs understand flavour, hygiene and kitchen pressure.

Many late starters progress faster than younger colleagues once they have learned the brewing basics, because they already know how to run a team or a project.

1. Test the idea: homebrew regularly with proper records for six months or more.
  2. Get floor time: spend weekends or leave helping in a local brewpub. Lift, clean and carry. See whether you enjoy it.
  3. Learn the science: take a structured course that fits around your job.
  4. Build savings: enough to cover the pay drop for a year or more.
  5. Talk to your family: agree on the risk and the hours together.
  6. Apply with a story: explain clearly why you are switching and what you bring.

Our guide to a brewing degree versus a short course helps with step three. For most mid-career switchers, a full degree is a big investment of time and money. Short, intensive courses plus practical experience often get you to a first job faster.

You do not have to start as an assistant brewer in a brewpub, although many people do. Depending on your background, you might enter as a QC technician, maintenance engineer, production planner or taproom manager, then move into brewing once you are inside.

Look at the full range of brewery jobs and match them to your existing skills. A role that values what you already know may pay better and give you a stronger start.

Physical work at 40 is not the same as at 22. Learn to lift correctly from the first day, use trolleys and lifting aids, wear good boots and drink plenty of water in hot brewhouses. Sleep matters when shifts start early.

Watch your stress too. Career changes are exciting and tiring. Give yourself time to adjust and do not judge the whole decision on a hard first month.

People who switch later usually say the best part is doing work they care about, making something people enjoy and learning every day. The hardest part is the first year, when you know less than everyone around you.

The ones who succeed prepare properly. They know the trade-offs, have savings, have tested the work and have learned the basics before applying. With that groundwork, starting a brewing career in your thirties or forties is a realistic plan rather than a gamble. What makes the biggest difference at interview is being able to talk about the brewing process with confidence, which is where structured study pays off.
faqs: Is 40 too old to become a brewer?
No. Many brewers started in their thirties or forties. Physical fitness, willingness to learn and good preparation matter more than age.
Will I have to take a pay cut?
Often, at least for an entry level brewing role. Planning savings for the first year or more makes the switch much less stressful.
Should I do a brewing degree as a mid-career switcher?
It depends on your goals and finances. Many switchers find short courses plus practical experience reach a first job faster than a full degree.
